summary: This package contains the data and Python code needed to reproduce every table and figure in Holgersson and Brown, “Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden’s Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas” (manuscript JFE-06-2026-0002, Journal of Forest Economics). The paper examines applications for permits to fell mountain-adjacent forest (fjällnära skog) in Sweden, which lies wholly within the reindeer husbandry area, around two 2020 court rulings: the Supreme Court’s Girjas judgment of 23 January 2020 (NJA 2020 s. 3), which recognised Sámi customary hunting and fishing rights, and the Land and Environment Court of Appeal’s judgment of 12 May 2020 (MÖD 2020:8), which established that owners refused a felling permit are entitled to compensation from the state. The analysis compares annual, monthly, county and municipal data on felling applications and notifications, and data on compensation paid for refused permits, to separate the effects of the two rulings. Data. All data are official statistics from the Swedish Forest Agency (Skogsstyrelsen), downloaded from its statistical database in October 2026 or supplied by its Statistics Unit: JO031402b.xlsx: applications for permits for regeneration felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by region and ownership category, 1995–2024 (number and hectares). JO031406.xlsx: applications for permits in mountain-adjacent forest, national, by month, 2008–2026. JO031401b.xlsx: notifications of regeneration felling, by county and ownership category, 1995–2025. These exclude the mountain-adjacent permit applications. JO031412.xlsx: notifications and applications for regeneration felling, by municipality and ownership category, 2010–2025. JO031405.xlsx: area notified or applied for, by county and month, 2007–2026. compensation_JO_table07.csv: compensation (intrångsersättning) paid for refused felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by county, 2020–2025 (number, SEK and hectares). This was transcribed from Skogsstyrelsen’s table “Intrångsersättning för nekad avverkning i fjällnära skog per län” (formal protection and compensation, table 07). Values shown as “..” in the source are suppressed for confidentiality. Code (Python 3). Run python run_all.py . It executes the scripts below in order and writes all results to the same folder: analysis.py: national and county results by ownership category, decomposition into number and size of applications, structural-break scan and Figure 1 (Tables 2 and 3). monthly.py: monthly comparison around the two rulings and Figure 2. parse_extra.py: reads the county, municipal and monthly notification tables. comparison.py: comparisons with ordinary felling in the reindeer husbandry area, including difference-in-differences estimates (Table 4). eventstudy.py: county–ownership pair estimates and Figure 3. compensation.py: compensation paid compared with area applied for (Table 5). Requirements: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels and openpyxl. All are pre-installed in Google Colab. Notes on derived series. Västerbotten is calculated as Norra Norrland minus Norrbotten. Mountain-adjacent forest in Södra Norrland lies in Jämtland. Dalarna is the national total minus Norra Norrland and Södra Norrland. National area for individual owners in 2024 is suppressed in the source and recovered as all owners minus other owners. Version note. This version replaces version 1 (10.5281/zenodo.17249309), which accompanied an earlier draft of the paper. All results in the revised paper were recomputed from the official source tables included here, and version 1 should no longer be used.

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement. The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun. DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here. SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience. STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

summary: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: Ensuring the provenance and authenticity of raw herbal materials in B2B supply chains requires integrating rapid species verification with immutable record-keeping. Existing centralized systems suffer from single-point trust vulnerability, while public blockchain architectures incur high gas fees and execution delays. This paper presents AyurAuth, a unified framework combining lightweight Edge-AI species classification using fine-tuned MobileNetV2 with a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric v2.x blockchain ledger. Deployed via a Node.js REST API and Flask microservice, AyurAuth achieves an empirical top-1 leaf classification accuracy of 85.00% (88.6 ms inference latency) across five key Ayurvedic herb species. Benchmark testing via Hyperledger Caliper demonstrates a peak write throughput of 408.47 TPS with a commit latency of 145.8 ms at 100 TPS, and a read throughput of 485.44 TPS at 41.5 ms latency with 100% success rate. End-to-end batch onboarding completes in 394.4 ms, while buyer QR verification queries execute in 28.5 ms without exposing internal ledger credentials.
title: AyurAuth: A Decentralized Edge-AI and Permissioned Blockchain Framework for Herbal Supply Chain Authenticity

summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. After deliberate termination of the PHP backend while nginx and static serving remained operational, 30/30 fallback requests succeeded and all 20/20 predesignated essential information items remained available, producing EIPR = 1.00 under the tested conditions. This result supports the narrow fallback-availability claim in the experimental configuration; it does not establish Internet-scale survivability, protocol security, or independent interoperability. A reproducibility archive containing raw results, configuration, logs and experiment artifacts accompanies this result. summary: Abstract Modern websites frequently depend on multi-layer dynamic software stacks comprising application runtimes, content-management systems, databases, frameworks, authentication services, third-party APIs, and cloud infrastructure. This architecture provides substantial functionality under normal conditions but can produce an undesirable failure mode: essential public information may become inaccessible even when networking, HTTPS, web servers, and the ability to serve static files remain operational. This paper introduces Web Lifeboat, an experimental architecture and protocol for cryptographically verifiable static fallback publishing. The design seeks to preserve a small, explicitly selected set of essential web information independently of the normal dynamic application stack. Emergency content is represented as static HTML accompanied by a signed manifest describing its identity, integrity, validity period, sequence, and associated trust information. Verification is designed to require neither the site’s database nor its application runtime and to remain meaningful when content is transferred through different transports. Web Lifeboat applies principles of graceful degradation and cyber resilience to web publishing: failure of high-complexity functionality should not necessarily imply failure of low-complexity, mission-essential information delivery. The current protocol draft, version 1.5.2, defines deterministic validation semantics, resource limits, rollback protections, cryptographic verification, key-state handling, clock-uncertainty behaviour, and transition rules. An internal conformance suite contains 42 package and trust-transition cases. The suite currently passes both its own validation process and a separate Go implementation from the same development lineage; genuinely independent implementation testing remains pending. In addition to the protocol design, this work introduces a measurable availability criterion, the Essential Information Preservation Ratio (EIPR), and reports a controlled local PHP-runtime failure experiment. summary: A falsifiable, typed model separates ontological categories, epistemic states, evidence, consensus, uncertainty, provenance, and authority. summary: Replication package for "Integration without crossing: Artificial intelligence and the organisation of research across disciplines" (Sung-Jong Lee, submitted to Quantitative Science Studies). The study uses OpenAlex works (CC0) published in 2020–2025 by authors in 22 university departments, identified from raw affiliation strings. It tests whether AI is dissolving disciplinary boundaries, forming a discipline of its own, or being absorbed by existing disciplines, and replicates the department-based Correlation Matrix of Major Disciplines of Schwartz, Park & Lee (2016). Contents: - code/: Python scripts for sampling and downloading works, text representations (TF-IDF, MiniLM, SPECTER2), alignment and crossing measures, AI absorption, third-layer fields, the 2016 CMMD replication, alternative AI definitions, and all figures. - data/sample_work_ids.csv: OpenAlex IDs, publication years and department codes of all sampled works. Titles and abstracts can be retrieved from OpenAlex. - data/analysis/: derived tables behind every table and figure in the paper. Paper-level score files and embeddings are not included because they can be regenerated with the code. - README.md: pipeline steps and run commands. - MANIFEST.csv: file list with sizes and SHA-256 checksums. Licences: derived data under CC BY 4.0; code under the MIT License (LICENSE-CODE.txt).
title: Replication package for "Integration without crossing: Artificial intelligence and the organisation of research across disciplines"

summary: This package contains the data and Python code needed to reproduce every table and figure in Holgersson and Brown, “Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden’s Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas” (manuscript JFE-06-2026-0002, Journal of Forest Economics). The paper examines applications for permits to fell mountain-adjacent forest (fjällnära skog) in Sweden, which lies wholly within the reindeer husbandry area, around two 2020 court rulings: the Supreme Court’s Girjas judgment of 23 January 2020 (NJA 2020 s. 3), which recognised Sámi customary hunting and fishing rights, and the Land and Environment Court of Appeal’s judgment of 12 May 2020 (MÖD 2020:8), which established that owners refused a felling permit are entitled to compensation from the state. The analysis compares annual, monthly, county and municipal data on felling applications and notifications, and data on compensation paid for refused permits, to separate the effects of the two rulings. Data. All data are official statistics from the Swedish Forest Agency (Skogsstyrelsen), downloaded from its statistical database in October 2026 or supplied by its Statistics Unit: JO031402b.xlsx: applications for permits for regeneration felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by region and ownership category, 1995–2024 (number and hectares). JO031406.xlsx: applications for permits in mountain-adjacent forest, national, by month, 2008–2026. JO031401b.xlsx: notifications of regeneration felling, by county and ownership category, 1995–2025. These exclude the mountain-adjacent permit applications. JO031412.xlsx: notifications and applications for regeneration felling, by municipality and ownership category, 2010–2025. JO031405.xlsx: area notified or applied for, by county and month, 2007–2026. compensation_JO_table07.csv: compensation (intrångsersättning) paid for refused felling in mountain-adjacent forest, by county, 2020–2025 (number, SEK and hectares). This was transcribed from Skogsstyrelsen’s table “Intrångsersättning för nekad avverkning i fjällnära skog per län” (formal protection and compensation, table 07). Values shown as “..” in the source are suppressed for confidentiality. Code (Python 3). Run python run_all.py . It executes the scripts below in order and writes all results to the same folder: analysis.py: national and county results by ownership category, decomposition into number and size of applications, structural-break scan and Figure 1 (Tables 2 and 3). monthly.py: monthly comparison around the two rulings and Figure 2. parse_extra.py: reads the county, municipal and monthly notification tables. comparison.py: comparisons with ordinary felling in the reindeer husbandry area, including difference-in-differences estimates (Table 4). eventstudy.py: county–ownership pair estimates and Figure 3. compensation.py: compensation paid compared with area applied for (Table 5). Requirements: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels and openpyxl. All are pre-installed in Google Colab. Notes on derived series. Västerbotten is calculated as Norra Norrland minus Norrbotten. Mountain-adjacent forest in Södra Norrland lies in Jämtland. Dalarna is the national total minus Norra Norrland and Södra Norrland. National area for individual owners in 2024 is suppressed in the source and recovered as all owners minus other owners. Version note. This version replaces version 1 (10.5281/zenodo.17249309), which accompanied an earlier draft of the paper. All results in the revised paper were recomputed from the official source tables included here, and version 1 should no longer be used.
title: Replication package for "Recognition Without Implementation: Property-Rights Compensation, Sámi Rights, and Felling Applications in Sweden's Mountain-Adjacent Forests after Girjas"

summary: This document defines a deterministic conformance profile and test-vector corpus for Evidence Qualification Receipts (EQRs). The profile, named eqr-core-1, makes receipt conformance mechanically reproducible: strict JSON structure, SHA-256 digest encoding, UTC timestamp handling, evidence-reference integrity, requirement-state derivation, and three-valued PASS, FAIL, or INDETERMINATE results are checked by a closed algorithm. The profile is intentionally narrow. Conformance does not establish that evidence is true, that a proposition is scientifically valid, that an issuer is trustworthy, or that an action is authorized. summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.

summary: TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS BIOLABORATORIES THROUGH MICROROBOTICS AND QUANTUM SENSING AT THE LIMIT Replayable Experiments x Permission Governance x External Metrology STARLI Research Institute XXIX - Flagship Research Monograph 20 Can an autonomous biolaboratory become scientifically useful without acquiring the authority to redefine its own permissions, validate its own evidence, or release untraceable measurements? This nonclinical research monograph investigates a bounded laboratory architecture connecting microrobotic sample handling, quantum-enabled and classical sensing, independent metrological reference chains, experiment replay, physical safe stopping, and human authority. Its central proposition is that reliable autonomy is a property of the entire evidence pathway rather than of any single robotic manipulator or AI model. A laboratory result is eligible for release only when sample identity and integrity, authorized execution, traceable references, justified uncertainty limits, and external acceptance are all demonstrated. An apparently successful action is not equivalent to a scientifically accepted sample. Digital replay does not replace physical replication, cryptographic event integrity does not guarantee sensor truth, and a quantum hardware label does not establish a practical sensing advantage. The research design is developed across 82 chapter-level inquiries with five independently paginated investigations per chapter, 30 connected mathematical research plates, 200 distinct Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The chapters address typed authority graphs, specimen provenance, sample exposure, closed-chip physics, covariance-aware sensing, AI planning within finite action spaces, common-cause fault injection, external interlocks, blinded classical benchmarks, evidence DAGs, cross-site replication, data retention, and responsible system retirement. The proposed minimum experimental prototype uses a closed microfluidic chip with interchangeable handling modules, two independently referenced readout channels, simulated or inert-tracer specimens, a separate audit service, and a physically verifiable stop mechanism. Proposed tests include unauthorized-action challenges, hidden calibration drift, interrupted events, sample contamination, unannounced network partitions, and independent laboratory replay or rerun. DOI-linked scientific references establish the relevant literature in automated laboratories, microrobotics, quantum sensing, uncertainty metrology, FAIR data stewardship, and computational reproducibility. They do not independently validate the integrated system proposed here. SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This book is a hypothesis-forming nonclinical research architecture. It reports no completed microrobotic or quantum biosensing experiments, no demonstrated clinical performance, no universal quantum advantage, and no autonomous system capable of authorizing itself. Statistical models, formulas, and decision policies require experimental verification, specialized review, and appropriate boundary conditions. A failed external reference, unavailable provenance chain, or revoked permission requires abstention rather than inference by convenience. STARLI RESEARCH PHILOSOPHY A trustworthy laboratory must remain answerable to evidence outside itself. Autonomy becomes scientifically meaningful when an experiment can be stopped, questioned, reconstructed, and handed to future researchers who retain the right to refuse its original assumptions.

summary: Version 2.0 preserves the original June 2026 Bridge Settlement manuscript and adds a separately dated October 2026 supplement. The addendum introduces Residual Strategic Optionality as an extension of Stakeholder Coherence Theory, examining the incentives of actors capable of disrupting negotiated settlements. It also compares the Bridge Settlement with Jeffrey Sachs's October 2026 peace framework for Ukraine, identifying areas of conceptual convergence and distinguishing the Bridge Settlement's emphasis on reciprocal economic interests, institutional participation, and self-reinforcing peace mechanisms. The original manuscript remains unchanged. This study develops a comparative Bayesian framework for evaluating natural zoonotic and research-associated hypotheses for the proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 under incomplete evidence. title: The Missing Bridge

summary: This archive provides the computational methods, structural coordinate files, source data, model outputs, and reproducibility documentation supporting an exploratory investigation of geometric persistence and prediction uncertainty at HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycan sites. The research examines whether local sequence divergence and sparse structural-context observations can improve the identification of unreliable glycan-site geometric predictions. The approach combines sequence-informed error estimation with residual information obtained from six observed glycan-site probes. Held-out evaluations included five BG505-derived Env structures and two JR-FL structures. In the original experiments, the six-probe method improved pooled dangerous-error discrimination relative to sequence-only prediction, with ROC AUC increasing from 0.704 to 0.945 in BG505 and from 0.522 to 0.761 in JR-FL. These results are exploratory. The original evaluations contained only two dangerous underestimates in BG505 and three in JR-FL. Within-structure discrimination did not consistently improve, and training-test construct overlap was identified. Additional construct-family exclusion analyses document the sensitivity of the findings to training composition and failure prevalence. The principal computational outputs were regenerated exactly from archived structural coordinates using the supplied scripts. The archive includes frozen protocols, structural data, prediction tables, provenance audits, family-exclusion analyses, and a companion manuscript draft. The study supports further investigation of sparse structural context for uncertainty assessment but does not establish reliable cross-strain site-level failure detection, glycan occupancy prediction, or protein synthesis prediction. This deposit is intended to support transparency, independent reproduction, methodological evaluation, and future extension of HIV-1 Env structural bioinformatics research. This research extends the author's previously deposited HIV-1 Env glycan-shield investigations by examining the predictive and uncertainty-assessment implications of geometric persistence, local structural constraints, and glycan-site organization.

summary: One annotation table for the alleles of the VarChAMP allele collection and the alleles assayed by Lacoste et al. 2024 (Cell, doi:10.1016/j.cell.2024.09.003) that are not in the collection: 8,963 alleles × 1,267 columns (8,619 collection , 344 lacoste , column allele_origin ). It is a lookup table for assay results: join the tested alleles on the key ( orf_id , mut_id , ccsb_mutation_id ). To describe the collection itself, filter allele_origin == "collection" . Built by the VarChAMP allele-metadata pipeline (GitHub: varchamp-allele-metadata, commit in metadata.json ) from the inputs record (lab data and snapshots, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23373387) and public resources pinned by checksum. metadata.json records the provenance of every input (origin, version, licence, checksum) and the QC counts of every step. Version 1.1 adds the measurements of three published studies of the lab (Sahni et al. 2015, Rolland et al. 2014, Luck et al. 2020), keyed on the same clone key, and a mapping of every study allele to the collection (file published_studies.zip ). The allele table is unchanged from version 1.0 (same files, same checksums). Files File Content varchamp_allele_metadata_public.parquet The table (Apache Parquet, with column types). varchamp_allele_metadata_public.tsv The same table as tab-separated text. metadata.json Provenance of every input, pipeline commit, per-step QC counts, the columns left out of this public release. published_studies.zip The published studies (folder published_studies/ ), two tables as Parquet and TSV: published_study_alleles (2,606 rows, one per study allele: the study's identifiers, its match to the collection — clone key, status , rule , gene, reference/alternate and position checks — and the per-allele readouts edgotype_class , chaperone_responsive and n_chaperones_expressed ) and published_study_edges (3,345 rows, one per allele × partner × study: Y2H from Sahni Table S3A, Rolland and Luck; WT rows flagged; the partner's Ensembl gene; each study's scores as published, in columns prefixed by study); metadata.json with the provenance and QC of the study steps. data_licences.md The terms of every source in the table and what they require. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md Copyright and permission notices of the MIT- and Apache-licensed scores. Columns The first 52 columns are a stable contract; definitions are in the pipeline's README. Identity: key, CCSB allele id, source collection, gene symbol, Ensembl gene and protein ids, ORF nucleotide and amino-acid change, SPDI and genomic position (GRCh38). Sequence confirmation: Y/N calls per clone (entry, DB, N2H, DUAL-IPA, mislocalisation); is_entry_seq_confirmed . ClinVar (variant_summary 2026-10): clinical significance (raw and cleaned categories), review status, phenotypes ( PhenotypeList , PhenotypeIDS ), OMIM numbers ( OMIM_IDs ). Protein coordinates: UniProt accession and the change on the UniProt canonical sequence. dbNSFP 5.0a (academic branch): 513 columns of variant scores and annotations for the matched transcript. Predictors: AlphaMissense ( am_pathogenicity ), SpliceAI ( splicing_variant ), ThermoMPNN ΔΔG on AlphaFold DB v6 models. Structure: pLDDT and relative solvent accessibility at the residue (AlphaFold DB v6 F1 model). Domains and features: TED domains and the hit at the variant (CATH v4.4.0 names); G2P protein features ( g2p_* ). Disease: mode of inheritance (GenCC, or Lacoste et al. 2024 Table S1 where GenCC's modes disagree), rare-disease modules of the gene (Buphamalai et al. 2021). Flags: is_synonymous , in_analysis_set . Published studies The studies' supplementary tables are pinned by publisher URL and checksum and kept as published; only the clone key ( orf_id , mut_id , ccsb_mutation_id ) is added. Matching to the collection: Study Alleles Matched Dropped by the collection's rules Unmapped Sahni et al. 2015 2,470 2,420 45 5 Rolland et al. 2014 115 114 1 0 Luck et al. 2020 21 21 0 0 Sahni: by the RC4 mutat

summary: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array     https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23575194 Abstract This paper develops a geometric analysis of vehicle-position observability when line-of-sight measurements are obtained from a surrounding beacon array. The vehicle is represented by an unknown Cartesian position, while each beacon contributes a unit line-of-sight vector. The associated Jacobian yields the Fisher information matrix, whose inverse supplies the Cramér–Rao bound on position covariance. In the horizontal plane, beacon directions determine the conditioning of the position estimate through their angular spread; in elevation, nonzero vertical separation supplies sensitivity to depth and suppresses the vertical dilution that occurs in a coplanar arrangement. Design implications are stated in terms of angular diversity, range, symmetry, and beacon elevation, and are formalized through the classical D- and E-optimality criteria. The treatment is first-order and analytical: no field calibration, stochastic measurement data, or performance claim beyond the stated linearized model is made. Index Terms —Beacon localization, Observability, Line-of-sight geometry, Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, Optimal experimental design, Position covariance, Vehicle navigation.
title: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array

The associated Jacobian yields the Fisher information matrix, whose inverse supplies the Cramér–Rao bound on position covariance. summary: Code, configuration, pre-registered protocol, frozen failure-cause codebook, prompts and aggregate results for an industrial case study of continuous integration (CI) failures. The study evaluates time-ordered prediction of CI run failures before they run, classifies failure causes into a nine-category taxonomy grouped by the owner of the fix, and compares a rule-based classifier, a text classifier and locally run open-weight language models (9 to 27 billion parameters) on confidential build-log excerpts, scored against the gold labels and an independent human rater. A before-and-after comparison of a migration between CI services is included as supplementary analysis. Every number, table and figure in the accompanying article is traced to a file in results/. The engineering records and log excerpts of the organisation studied are confidential and are not included; docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.md describes their structure so that the procedure can be repeated on other data. The rule set is withheld at the data owner's request; src/rules_template.yaml shows its format. Code and configuration: Apache License 2.0. Documents, tables and figures: CC BY 4.0.
title: Replication package for: Predicting and diagnosing continuous integration failures in an industrial organisation with locally run language models

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A random walk is robust if an adversary who may change every transition probability by a small relative amount cannot make it much slower to reach its targets. Zuckerman (Markov chain robustness, ITCS 2026, LIPIcs 362, 118) conjectured that the largest safe relative change is at least a constant divided by the graph's diameter (Conjecture 1.16). This package shows the conjecture is false. A graph can have short routes that the walk almost never uses; a small fixed bias away from a target accumulates between rare visits to them and depletes the target's stationary mass, and Kac's formula turns this into a long hitting time. For explicit cubic graphs J_b on N vertices with diameter O(log N), every effective resistance is at most 684 (proof), and a fixed perturbation of size 1/b, with error times diameter tending to zero, multiplies the worst-case hitting time by a factor of order b; the robustness is O(N^(-1/3)). For explicit 3m-regular graphs of diameter exactly three, the mixing time is at most 50(m+1), so with Zuckerman's mixing-time theorem the robustness lies between constant multiples of N^(-1/2) and N^(-1/4) (proof; not matching). An exact computation shows a 5.80-fold slowdown on a 5,995-vertex member with error times diameter 0.74. A diameter-two example, a reversible-perturbation bound and a comparison with Kemeny's constant are included. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), seven verification scripts with a driver that reproduces the reference JSON results byte for byte under python -B -O, semantic negative controls, figures and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; exact checks; producer-side replay including a clean replay in a separate copy; internal AI-assisted review, AI-assisted adversarial reviews (OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol; Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5; OpenAI gpt-6-astra) and a verification re-review. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Small diameter does not control hitting-time robustness

summary: We extend the Deep Hough Transform (DHT), which detects semantic lines by aggregating learned features along candidate lines into a two-dimensional parameter space, to higher-dimensional parametric curve families. The extension is hard because the accumulator for a family with d parameters has O(B^d) cells for B bins per axis. We propose a factorized deep Hough transform, a differentiable feature-space voting cascade that splits the parameter vector into a spatial anchor and a shape. A coarse two-dimensional accumulator votes for anchors, and a dense shape accumulator is built only around the top-k anchors, so memory falls from O(B^d) to O(B^d1 + k B^d2). Lines are the degenerate case with no second stage. We also define a curve agreement score that extends the EA line similarity to parametric curves, and a synthetic benchmark of parabolas, circles and ellipses with noise, occlusion and distractors. We evaluate with thresholds selected on a validation split and the test split scored once, and we give the geometric baselines the same treatment. Under this protocol the choice of Stage-1 pooling over probe shapes matters a great deal: max pooling raises parabola F from 0.51 to 0.70 over log-sum-exp (3 seeds). With it, the cascade ties a tuned RANSAC fit on parabolas (0.706 vs. 0.702) and circles (0.743 vs. 0.742) and is slightly behind it on ellipses (0.382 vs. 0.410), while direct regression and query-based heads reach 0.15 and 0.13 on parabolas. So the cascade is competitive with classical fitting rather than better than it, and its practical advantage is memory: at B=32 a dense d=5 accumulator would need about 4 GB (computed, not instantiated) against a measured 236 KB for the cascade. We locate the remaining error in Stage 1. Running Stage 2 at the ground-truth anchors gives F = 0.938 against 0.706, and curves whose anchors lie within about 8 pixels of each other lose about 0.2 F because their Stage-1 peaks merge. We also report a TuSimple lane-detection stress test, which we treat as a feasibility check rather than a competitive result. Code and the benchmark generator are released.

summary: PFAS-CAST (PFAS Censoring-Aware Screening Tool) is a browser-based and Python companion tool for exploratory PFAS benchmark screening. It applies the primary censored-likelihood multiple-imputation engine from Kharel, G., Kirilenko, A. P., Harvey, O. R., and Zou, C. B., “Censoring-aware models quantify systematic underestimation of PFAS occurrence in US drinking-water monitoring,” Cell Reports Sustainability (2026), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100893 , to user-supplied PFAS monitoring data and configurable benchmark thresholds. PFAS-CAST is an exploratory screening and prioritization companion, not a regulatory-compliance tool. Please cite the paper when using the tool. Version 1.1.1 (October 2026): updated citation to the published paper; added automatic recognition of EPA UCMR 5 Data Finder column names and tab-delimited files in both the browser and Python tools; fixed two browser-tool parsing defects (a missing detect-flag column caused all rows to be treated as non-detects, and SamplingLocationID was not recognized). The statistical engine is unchanged. The package includes the standalone browser tool, the Python companion and engine, method references, a QA note, a checksum manifest, and two test input files.

summary: AUTONOMOUS QUANTUM BIOSENSOR DRIFT DIAGNOSIS AND RECOVERY AT THE LIMIT Drift Identifiability × Reference Transfer × Safe Requalification STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 06 Can an autonomous quantum-enabled biosensing platform distinguish genuine specimen changes from thermal response, optical ageing, clock instability, reference-source drift, and permanent component degradation? More importantly, can the platform recognize when calibration is insufficient and an instrument must remain outside the scientific measurement process? This research monograph develops a hypothesis-forming, nonclinical framework for autonomous biosensor drift diagnosis, independently traceable reference transfer, and evidence-based recovery decisions. Its central scientific distinction is between making an instrument appear numerically stable and demonstrating that the instrument has genuinely regained acceptable measurement performance. The proposed architecture combines state-space estimation, controlled environmental perturbations, independent measurement references, multivariate uncertainty analysis, quantum sensing physics, classical sensor comparisons, and verifiable calibration governance. Particular attention is given to the identifiability problem: a mathematical model may separate sample and instrument states in its equations without possessing sufficient experimental information to distinguish them in reality. The 771-page volume contains 82 research chapters, 410 independently paginated investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical research plates, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Major research directions include nitrogen-vacancy diamond resonance thermometry, photon-counting uncertainty, ODMR spectral interpretation, optical contrast degradation, thermal hysteresis, frequency-reference instability, material ageing, common-mode reference failure, blind fault injection, calibration transfer, immutable measurement histories, and independent instrument requalification. Each chapter establishes a specific technical mechanism, a competing explanation, an experimental intervention, and conditions under which its proposed interpretation should be rejected. The 200 Research Gates preserve falsifiable research questions, proposed experimental methods, measurable outcomes, independent comparators, uncertainty-aware acceptance conditions, and evidence-preserving stopping procedures. The 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos introduce provisional research architectures that future human and AI investigators may challenge, modify, reconstruct, or replace. Seventeen DOI-linked scientific publications and metrological standards provide foundations in quantum sensing, sensor drift compensation, statistical state estimation, and measurement uncertainty. These references support established physical principles and methodological approaches. They do not constitute experimental validation of the proposed integrated STARLI F06 system. summary: Gratitude can concern a benefit received, a harm that did not occur, or the conditions that make one's own assumptions examinable. We develop the proposal that appreciating these conditions can orient practice toward realizing emptiness: examining how distinctions arise, relinquishing their assumed intrinsic necessity, and retaining their conditional usefulness. The argument distinguishes an observed absence, a missing observation, counterfactual valuation and non-reification, and places their differences in dialogue with explicitly situated philosophical and scriptural sources. We reconstruct Fisher, Sandved Smith and Hohwy's gratitude and gaze notebooks, then separate faithful reconstruction from corrected experiments and new mechanisms. GNN-declared paired recall experiments use 5120 independent agent-world units, matched environmental exposure and replay dose, normalized likelihoods, and independent predictive assessment. Pinned Realizing Emptiness interfaces supply structural admission and finite mathematical comparators. An enacted inquiry model separates appreciation, costly activity, access to alternatives and evidence-responsive retention or revision; explicit learning-to-gaze and joint scene/encoding experiments examine transfer and identifiability. Exact count enumeration, mathematical nulls, paired controls and joint bootstrap inference make the resulting software claims independently checkable. Selective positive recall reduces the declared optimism summary, while its predictive consequences depend on the world mixture and the specified transfer bridge. Counterfactual absence valuation preserves inference by construction. Accessible inquiry can revise a contradicted restriction and retain a useful one; activity without access instead incurs costs while preserving rigid forecasts. Exact analysis exposes rare adverse selections absent from seeded realizations. The original gaze code reproduces the pre-intervention occupancy but contains no implemented after intervention. Our active-scene extension finds a context-dependent access advantage without an additional inquiry-specific predictive advantage. Joint scene/encoding inquiry distinguishes learning an encoding from combining it with scene evidence: observationally equivalent labels remain unidentifiable, and excluded hypotheses cannot be recovered. Known-answer fixtures also retain skew-related undercoverage and unavailable rare-event estimates rather than treating replication size as a remedy for every inferential failure. The contribution is a reproducible account of enabling operations and their limits, together with a falsifiable human research program that separates inquiry value from patience, anticipated good news and instrumental information demand. Synthetic model results establish neither human gratitude nor contemplative realization or clinical benefit. Code, declared models and reproducibility materials are available at github.com/docxology/thanks_for_nothing .

summary: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. Language: English Research Type: Conceptual and Methodological Research Monograph Edition

The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. Language: English Research Type: Conceptual and Methodological Research Monograph Edition: Version 1.0, October 2026 Research Program: STARLI / White Rainbow Epoch

summary: Amun Code is an open-source parallel simulation code for astrophysical fluids and plasmas. It solves the equations of hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics in two and three dimensions on uniform or adaptively refined Cartesian meshes. Supported formulations include Newtonian flows with isothermal or adiabatic equations of state, and special relativistic hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics. The code uses Godunov-type shock-capturing methods with selectable approximate Riemann solvers, high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory and monotonicity-preserving reconstruction, and Runge–Kutta time integration. Embedded integrators provide error-based time-step control. Magnetic-divergence errors are controlled through generalized Lagrange multiplier cleaning. Optional viscosity, magnetic resistivity, and stochastic turbulence driving support studies of turbulence, shocks, and magnetic reconnection. Driving options include the Alvelius method and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Amun Code is written primarily in modern Fortran and supports hybrid MPI/OpenMP parallelization. Simulation settings are supplied through parameter files, and outputs use native XML/binary or HDF5 formats. AmunPy provides a separate Python interface for reading simulation data. The code is developed by Grzegorz Kowal and distributed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later.

summary: When a central bank raises rates, the government's interest bill rises. Whether the extra interest supports domestic demand depends on who receives it. Recent evidence finds this direct fiscal channel of monetary policy was small in the United States before 2020, because long Treasury maturities slowed the pass-through of policy rates to interest costs. We argue that this conclusion does not carry over to the post-2022 tightening. Quantitative easing replaced long-term Treasury debt with overnight interest-bearing reserves, so the consolidated public sector repriced far faster than Treasury maturities suggest, and the price-insensitive official holders that once anchored demand for Treasuries were replaced at the margin by domestic private buyers. Using published Treasury, Federal Reserve and TIC data, we decompose the rise in public-sector interest outflows between 2021 and 2024. Net interest rose by about \$530 billion, three quarters of it due to higher rates rather than more debt. Counting the Treasury and the Federal Reserve together, roughly 57 percent of the increase in public-sector interest outflows reached domestic non-federal holders directly, 27 percent reached them through the Federal Reserve's payments on reserves and reverse repos, whose counterpart was the end of its remittances to the Treasury, and 16 percent went abroad. For the Treasury securities the Federal Reserve held at the end of 2021, quantitative easing made higher rates reach non-federal holders' income roughly two to two and a half times as fast as if the bonds had stayed in private hands. Domestic investors absorbed close to 90 percent of the growth in privately held debt. We discuss what this implies for the potency of rate hikes, for the design of interest on reserves, and for reserve-currency issuers more generally.
title: Who Receives the Interest? Reserve Status, Holder Composition and the Fiscal Channel of Monetary Policy

Recent evidence finds this direct fiscal channel of monetary policy was small in the United States before 2020, because long Treasury maturities slowed the pass-through of policy rates to interest costs. We argue that this conclusion does not carry over to the post-2022 tightening. Quantitative easing replaced long-term Treasury debt with overnight interest-bearing reserves, so the consolidated public sector repriced far faster than Treasury maturities suggest, and the price-insensitive official holders that once anchored demand for Treasuries were replaced at the margin by domestic private buyers. Using published Treasury, Federal Reserve and TIC data, we decompose the rise in public-sector interest outflows between 2021 and 2024. Net interest rose by about \$530 billion, three quarters of it due to higher rates rather than more debt. Counting the Treasury and the Federal Reserve together, roughly 57 percent of the increase in public-sector interest outflows reached domestic non-federal holders directly, 27 percent reached them through the Federal Reserve's payments on reserves and reverse repos, whose counterpart was the end of its remittances to the Treasury, and 16 percent went abroad. For the Treasury securities the Federal Reserve held at the end of 2021, quantitative easing made higher rates reach non-federal holders' income roughly two to two and a half times as fast as if the bonds had stayed in private hands. Domestic investors absorbed close to 90 percent of the growth in privately held debt. We discuss what this implies for the potency of rate hikes, for the design of interest on reserves, and for reserve-currency issuers more generally.

title: Who Receives the Interest? Reserve Status, Holder Composition and the Fiscal Channel of Monetary Policy

summary: EFGB MATLAB Simulator v1.0.0 Initial research software release | MATLAB R2024a This release provides the MATLAB implementation of Energy-Feasibility-Guaranteed Bidding (EFGB): for decentralized task allocation among heterogeneous UAVs under battery constraints and lossy communication. Associated manuscript: EFGB: Team-Independent Round-Trip Energy Admission for Decentralized Multi-UAV Rescue Allocation under Lossy Communication (submitted to Robotics and Autonomous Systems). Features Team-independent round-trip energy admission with capacity-bounded workload charges. Capacity-proportional workload sharing and reserve-aware mission admission. Gilbert–Elliott communication modeling with lossy awards and acknowledgments. Comparative policies including outbound-only admission, reactive safety override, SGA, the earlier conference auction, and CBBA. SGA + EFGB and CBBA + EFGB for separating allocation-protocol effects from the safety admission rule. Experiments covering ablations, docking-order validation, communication degradation, energy-model mismatch, deadlines, and robustness. Physics-based and flight-data-derived energy-error evaluation. Included evidence revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/ : final SigLIP2 MIL ensemble versus random forest, stratified into 278 one-photo, 127 two-photo and 345 three-photo cases; 10,000 paired case-bootstrap draws, confidence intervals, multiplicity adjustments, raw subgroup scores and a publication figure. revision-experiments/10_test_discrepancy/ : reproduction of seven paired macro ROC-AUC DeLong-type comparisons and the historical permutation tests, with a separate rank-scale sensitivity analysis. The primary raw-score permutation remains non-significant (p=0.089891); the macro DeLong-type p=0.000072328 and rank sensitivity answer different null questions. Modules 07 (chance-anchored AP) and 08 (paired AUC), added after the original v1.0.0 snapshot, are now included in the release alongside modules 09 and 10. Saved predictions and analysis inputs remain tracked in Git. Copy manifests verify the original E1/E2 script and result bytes. The manuscript-workspace copies remain unchanged. Correct model identity and availability The final manuscript predictor is the canonical SigLIP2 MIL ensemble of seeds 42–51, followed by validation-fitted per-condition Platt calibration. Its saved test predictions are artifacts/models/mil/siglip2_so400m/canonical/ensemble/test_predictions.csv and reproduce approximately 0.851 macro ROC-AUC and 0.304 macro average precision on the locked 750 cases. The separately fitted final model and earlier ensembles are different predictors. The Hugging Face public HawkFranklin-Research/pelliscope-siglip2-mil and private HawkFranklin-Research/pelliscope-25class-models-internal repositories contain historical 20 September weights. Their cards were explicitly labeled as earlier versions on 23 October; commit receipts are in v1.1.0-huggingface-receipts.json . No weights were changed or represented as the final ensemble. Final September 27 checkpoints are not included in this code release, and their recovery/upload remains pending. Google Cloud access currently requires renewed authentication; VM contents have not been verified in this release session. Reproduce the new analyses From the repository root, in the project environment: python revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/analyze.py --code-root . python revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/plot_results.py python revision-experiments/10_test_discrepancy/verify_tests.py --code-root . These commands use saved predictions only. They require neither model checkpoints nor feature banks. See each module README for sparse-label, subgroup and test-null limitations. No causal advantage from multi-image aggregation or clinical benefit is established by these analyses alone. Archive continuity The previous immutable archive is v1.0.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23000066 ; its version-series DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23000065 . The new GitHub release is intended as the next version of that archive. Do not cite the old version-specific DOI as containing these new modules; verify the new version record before updating a manuscript citation.

summary: Makes canu failures fatal when canu itself could not run. Previously any canu failure during read correction was reported as "This probably means there is low depth, don't be too concerned" and plassembler carried on with uncorrected reads - including when one of canu 's own jobs could not run at all. In the Biocontainers image, canu 's generated job scripts call expr -- ... , which the image's BusyBox expr rejects, so k-mer counting failed every time; continuing with uncorrected reads left Unicycler assembling 110 spurious contigs that the depth filter then had to discard. Thanks @ SieurRicort for the detailed report and diagnosis ( #92 ) plassembler now reads canu 's log to tell its stops apart. A job that failed ( ... jobs failed, tried 2 times, giving up. ) or an internal canu crash stops the run, reports the failing stage alongside canu 's own output, and keeps the canu directory, which holds each job's log. Low read coverage - the expected outcome for a sample with no plasmids - still carries on as before, now with a message saying so. Any other stop also carries on, but shows canu 's reason rather than reassurance. The same applies to canu assembly with --canu_flag
title: gbouras13/plassembler: v1.8.6

Opening example is from an earlier task set; spatial-set results use the models named above. Repository: https://github.com/SchrodingersCattt/crystalsight

Henrique - Sílvia Faria (ORCID: 0000-0002-7672-3972) — ISCAP, Instituto Politécnico do Porto; REMIT, Universidade Portucalense **Funding:** FCT — Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia, grant UID/05105/2025 **Target journal:** Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans (Elsevier) **Corresponding author:** Prof. Victor Santos — vsantos@iscac.pt **License:** Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) **Version:** v3.0.0 (2026-10-22) — supersedes v2.0.0 (2026-10-21) and v1.0.0 (2026-05-25) **What's new in v3.0.0 (2026-10-22):** the structured review of the five focal constructs (Scopus and Web of Science, 2025–2026) was reclassified. The 148-record list of v2.0.0 was re-read at abstract level by a single reviewer on 22 October 2026: only 87 studies compare an artificial agent empirically with a human presenter or influencer, and they form the final corpus (61 excluded: 38 artificial agents only; 15 reviews, bibliometric or conceptual papers; 4 analytical models without consumer data; 4 comparisons of AI-controlled with human-controlled avatars). Final flow: 1,292 → 890 → 518 → 87 (Q1 = 78, Q2 = 9; 2025 = 26, 2026 = 61; 87/87 DOI verified). New files: (1) Appendix_A_Corpus_87.csv — final corpus; (2) Reclassificacao_Corpus_148.xlsx — decision and reason for each of the 148 records; (3) PRISMA_2020_Flow_EN_87.png — study-selection flow; (4) Strings_pesquisa_WoS_Scopus.txt — search strings; (5) Scopus_records_n533.csv and WoS_records_n759.csv — record lists of the database exports (authors, title, year, source, DOI, EID/UT; abstracts are not redistributed); (6) Corpus_ambito_Q1Q2_n518.csv — the 518 records eligible on quartile and scope; (7) README.md — updated. Removed from this version (still available in v2.0.0): Appendix_A_Corpus_148.csv (superseded by the 87-study corpus) and Manuscript_Atualizado_2025-2026.pdf (the manuscript is under revision). Note on Synthetic_Sample_Parameters_v14_N500.xlsx (sheet Tab5, section C): the source column attributes the Phase 1 structural path values to a "conservative median" of studies in the earlier PRISMA synthesis; no documented calculation of that median exists. The values are design values set at the design stage: their direction and relative ordering follow the theoretical expectations of the model, their magnitudes were set to plausible moderate-to-strong values and were not derived from a quantitative synthesis of the reviewed studies. They are used only to check model identification, parameter recovery and power. The file is kept unchanged for transparency. Empirical data (n = 145) and all reported empirical results are unchanged. --- ## Overview This Zenodo deposit contains all materials required to reproduce, audit, and extend the empirical findings reported in the manuscript "Human vs. AI Avatar Presenters in B2C Product Demonstrations: Trust, Engagement, and Purchase Intention" submitted to the Journal Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. Because the Zenodo web interface does not preserve folder hierarchy on upload, all files appear in a single flat list. Matches Appendix B of the manuscript. | | `SmartPLS_Human_n145.csv` | Phase 2 — Human

summary: AI is becoming pervasive in everyday life, appearing as a visible and constant presence in many aspects of work, education, and personal relationships. It restructures job markets, creates new slop aesthetics, and is forcibly incorporated into almost all digital services with promises of economic growth and efficiency, without any serious reflection on the social and political consequences. But we believe that the situation is not hopeless or settled, no matter how powerful the corporations or systems profiting from AI may appear. The trick is to recognize that democratic levers for change are not given in advance, but must be actively and creatively reimagined. This collection of essays is a survey of where such handles are hiding in the digital age, in places considerably less obvious than a county hearing. In procurement, in a watershed boundary, in a tax treaty almost nobody knows exists, in a benchmark written by users rather than engineers, or in a legal assumption about how technology “works” that is ripe for challenging. None of these were designed as democratic instruments, which is precisely the point. Democracy is presented not as a form of government but a way of living, and as a skill that can be practiced. The authors reflect on an emergent, collective argument about the different meanings and possibilities of “digital democracy from below.” They go beyond the U.S. context to explore distinct but interdependent dynamics of technological politics in places around the world. The collection has five sections: (1) Seeing through the fog; (2) Recognizing the limits of infrastructure; (3) Fighting erasure; (4) Practicing everyday democracy; and (5) Resisting, organizing and re-building. It also offers a roadmap for organizing participatory workshops that can adapted and reused. Contributors (alphabetical order by last name): Rafael C. Alvarado, Brianne Anderson, Nicole West Bassoff, Luã Cruz, Aashka Dave, Nancy L. Deutsch, Laurent Dubois, Joshua Earle, MC Forelle, Matthew Gillikin, Sergio Guillen Grillo, Yujia He, Mar Hicks, Steven L. Francisco, Spencer Phillips, Jess Reia, Karina Ripley, Andrea Roberts, Fernanda R. Rosa, Dhanaraj Thakur, Quito Tsui, Michael Tyrala, Jonathan van Geuns, Yingchong Wang, Megan Wiessner, Rebecca Williams, Bianca Wylie, Caitlin D. Wylie.

title: Digital Democracy from Below: Resisting AI and Techno-solutionism

summary: AI is becoming pervasive in everyday life, appearing as a visible and constant presence in many aspects of work, education, and personal relationships. It restructures job markets, creates new slop aesthetics, and is forcibly incorporated into almost all digital services with promises of economic growth and efficiency, without any serious reflection on the social and political consequences. But we believe that the situation is not hopeless or settled, no matter how powerful the corporations or systems profiting from AI may appear. The trick is to recognize that democratic levers for change are not given in advance, but must be actively and creatively reimagined. This collection of essays is a survey of where such handles are hiding in the digital age, in places considerably less obvious than a county hearing. In procurement, in a watershed boundary, in a tax treaty almost nobody knows exists, in a benchmark written by users rather than engineers, or in a legal assumption about how technology “works” that is ripe for challenging. None of these were designed as democratic instruments, which is precisely the point. Democracy is presented not as a form of government but a way of living, and as a skill that can be practiced. The authors reflect on an emergent, collective argument about the different meanings and possibilities of “digital democracy from below.” They go beyond the U.S. context to explore distinct but interdependent dynamics of technological politics in places around the world. The collection has five sections: (1) Seeing through the fog; (2) Recognizing the limits of infrastructure; (3) Fighting erasure; (4) Practicing everyday democracy; and (5) Resisting, organizing and re-building. It also offers a roadmap for organizing participatory workshops that can adapted and reused. Contributors (alphabetical order by last name): Rafael C. summary: We develop a simple Lorentz-covariant construction of the Born--Infeld-type cubic interactions $(s, s_1, s_2)$ of massless higher-spin fields with $s + s_1 + s_2$ derivatives in four-dimensiona flat space. For arbitrary spins $s \ge s_1 \ge s_2$, the vertex is formulated in terms of a conserved higher-spin current and its trace. In contrast to the famous Berends--Burgers--van Dam currents, these currents are constructed from higher-spin Weyl tensors of a single chirality, schematically $J \sim \partial C \partial C$. Starting with a general ansatz, we derive recurrence relations fixing the current coefficients, identify the unique non-trivial conserved current after eliminating trivial (fake) vertices, and show that in the range $s \le s_1 + s_2$ the interaction admits a manifestly gauge-invariant representation in terms of higher-spin Weyl tensors. The construction is then extended to $\mathcal{N}=1$ and $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetry using the corresponding off-shell superfield formalisms. In the $\mathcal{N}=1$ case, we obtain the general conserved integer superspin $s$ supercurrent with manifest supersymmetry, which is bilinear in the Weyl supertensors of superspins $Y_1$ and $Y_2$. For identical superfields, $Y_1 = Y_2$, this supercurrent vanishes for odd $s$ and is in agreement with earlier results by Gates and Koutrolikos. In the $\mathcal{N}=2$ case, using harmonic superspace, we construct the principal higher-spin supercurrent whose coefficients are uniquely fixed by the conservation equations. In contrast to the $\mathcal{N}=0,1$ cases, for identical $\mathcal{N}=2$ superfields, the corresponding vertex does not vanish. The results provide a systematic framework for Born--Infeld-type higher-spin interactions and their supersymmetric extensions.

summary: NovaFabric is self-hosted, open-source replay and evidence infrastructure for AI agents and agentic systems. It captures agent executions as portable, secret-scanned Run Capsules and provides replay, behavioral and structural diff, lineage, cryptographic provenance, assurance, and audit around those executions. The same capture layer can wrap general commands and runs entirely in the user's own infrastructure, from local environments through Kubernetes to SLURM/HPC, with no accounts and no telemetry. It is built around five primitives — Asset Registry, Run Capsule, Replay, Lineage, and Evidence Bundle — and five explicit replay modes (forensic, mocked, semantic, exact, and the experimental intervention mode). Run Capsules can be sealed with the user’s own key; sealing is opt-in. Evidence bundles verify offline using only sha256sum and an ed25519 verifier, with no NovaFabric installation required. Interoperates with established specifications rather than inventing formats: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, in-toto/DSSE, RFC 3161 timestamping, W3C PROV, OpenLineage, and CycloneDX.

summary: What work appears around a public mathematics release? This article follows five selected GitHub repository versions containing navigation tools, checking records, bibliography additions, explanatory corrections and conditional mathematical development. It distinguishes carried material, changes relative to a specified version and declared focus. Three observations trace repository membership on 9, 15 and 22 October 2026, while genealogy and overlapping activity views reveal different relationships. A separate documentary pilot examines later method adaptation, conditional application and explanatory reuse. The findings identify inspectable public work and particular subsequent connections, with explicit limits on mathematical validation, representativeness and measured benefit.
title: Tracking the Ripple Effect of OpenAI Mathematics on GitHub

summary: Learnable Representations (LRs) can fit parametric families of functions to diverse kinds of signals. These emergent neural-native data formats are gathering interest in the scientific community due to their compactness, resolution-agnosticism and amenability to direct neural processing. On the other hand, gigapixel images are becoming increasingly widespread across a variety of scientific, cultural, and industrial domains. In this paper, we present GigaBench, the first benchmark and experimental evaluation focused on deploying LRs with gigapixel imagery. GigaBench includes images collected, acquired, and synthetically rendered across diverse domains, and addresses image compression and super-resolution. We adapt a representative set of LRs, spanning Implicit, Hybrid, and Explicit methods, so as to operate reliably at the gigapixel scale on consumer hardware. Through systematic evaluation across reconstruction quality, model size, compression and inference times, we identify consistent trends across methods and suggest actionable guidance for future investigation.
title: GigaBench: Benchmarking Learnable Representations for Gigapixel Image Compression and Super-Resolution
